The core idea is to address the limitations of single-prompt approaches, which often fail to capture the inherent visual variance within a class. APPLe leverages a large language model (LLM), specifically GPT-3, to generate diverse prompts for each class, effectively creating a 'class prototype' that represents the various visual manifestations of that class. To further refine these prototypes, the authors introduce an adaptive attention mechanism. This mechanism assigns higher weights to 'representative' prototypes, which are identified by averaging the cosine similarities of all prototypes within a class and selecting those that are most similar to this average. This attention mechanism aims to focus on the most informative visual representations when computing the final class embedding. Additionally, a prototype decorrelation loss is incorporated to reduce the influence of co-occurring multiple prototypes, which is particularly beneficial in scenarios where visual samples are biased or limited. The method is evaluated on several tasks, including generalization to unseen classes, new target datasets, and domain generalization. The experimental results demonstrate that APPLe consistently outperforms existing methods, including CoOp, ProDA, PLOT, MaPLe, and CoCoOp, on various benchmarks. The authors also conduct an ablation study to analyze the impact of the number of prototypes on performance. Overall, the paper presents a simple yet effective method for adapting VLMs to downstream tasks by leveraging multiple prompts and an adaptive attention mechanism, achieving state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks.
